clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in KCNT1, which encodes the sodium-activated potassium channel Slack (KNa1.1) that regulates neuronal firing and the slow afterhyperpolarisation
Almost all pathogenic variants are gain-of-function, increasing potassium current in a way that paradoxically enhances network excitability
The two most recognised phenotypes are epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures and autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor (nocturnal frontal lobe) epilepsy
The migrating focal seizure phenotype presents in early infancy with near-continuous multifocal seizures that shift between hemispheres on electroencephalography and severe developmental impairment
The sleep-related hypermotor phenotype can be familial, with clusters of brief nocturnal motor seizures, and may be associated with psychiatric and cognitive comorbidity
Quinidine has been trialled as a targeted blocker of the gain-of-function channel, but clinical responses have been inconsistent and it requires cardiac monitoring
Seizures are frequently drug-resistant, and multidisciplinary supportive care is central to management
reference.pathophysiology: KCNT1 encodes Slack (KNa1.1), a sodium-activated potassium channel that contributes to the slow afterhyperpolarisation and shapes the timing and adaptation of neuronal firing. Pathogenic variants are predominantly gain-of-function, producing constitutively increased potassium current. Although greater potassium conductance might be expected to dampen activity, in affected networks it disrupts normal firing patterns and inhibitory balance, promoting the intense multifocal or frontal-predominant seizures seen clinically. The gain-of-function mechanism underlies the rationale for quinidine, which partially blocks the channel, though its clinical utility has proven variable.
additionalDifferentials: SCN2A and SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
CHRNA4/CHRNB2 autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy
DEPDC5 and other GATOR1 familial focal epilepsies
Structural focal epilepsy from focal cortical dysplasia
Other genetic causes of epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to confirm the KCNT1 variant
Prolonged video electroencephalography to demonstrate migrating multifocal ictal patterns or nocturnal frontal seizures
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude a structural lesion
Electrocardiography and cardiac assessment before and during any quinidine trial
Family history and segregation analysis in dominant sleep-related hypermotor cases
redFlags: Continuous or near-continuous migrating seizures with developmental arrest in infancy
Cardiac conduction abnormalities, especially with quinidine exposure
Sudden clustering of nocturnal seizures with injury risk
reference.prognosis: The migrating focal seizure phenotype generally has a poor outcome with refractory seizures and severe developmental impairment, whereas the sleep-related hypermotor phenotype varies from relatively mild to disabling, sometimes with significant psychiatric and cognitive comorbidity.
pitfalls: Expecting a uniform quinidine response, when benefit is inconsistent and requires careful cardiac monitoring
Assuming a potassium-channel gain-of-function must reduce excitability rather than disrupt network firing
Missing the familial nature of the sleep-related hypermotor phenotype and failing to counsel relatives
Mislabelling nocturnal hypermotor seizures as parasomnias
references: ILAE resources on epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures and sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy
management: Trial of quinidine as a targeted blocker of the gain-of-function channel in selected cases, recognising inconsistent responses and the need for cardiac monitoring
Broad-spectrum antiseizure medications for the migrating focal seizures, which are typically drug-resistant
Adjunctive options such as cannabidiol and consideration of the ketogenic diet for refractory seizures
Electrocardiography and cardiac surveillance for QT prolongation before and during any quinidine trial
Seizure control for the sleep-related hypermotor phenotype, with attention to associated psychiatric and cognitive comorbidity
Multidisciplinary developmental support and intensive care with rescue planning for the severe migrating focal seizure phenotype
Clinical genetics counselling, including segregation analysis in autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor families
